item.base_system: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (NPs) with mean diameter 4.5 nm, composition ≈Au20Co28Cu11Ni20Pt21, FCC structure, multi-twinned/icosahedral shape
item.intervention: Heating from 298 K to 473 K for 15 min
item.processing: In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating on SiN membrane, heating rate 1 K s⁻¹
item.test_conditions: 298 K to 473 K, vacuum, 15 min hold
item.structure_change: No change in particle size distribution; NPs retain original shape and structure
item.property_change: No change in size distribution; particle density unchanged
item.attributed_mechanism: Thermo-activated growth mechanisms not yet active below 673 K
quotes: Particle size distribution remains unchanged at 473 K but it is impacted when the temperature reaches 673 K
The size of NPs may also be slightly affected by Ostwald ripening, but as the dissolution of small nanoparticles was never observed during the in situ heating experiments
Prior to heating, the composition of individual NPs was measured by energy dispersive X‐ray spectroscopy (EDS) in STEM mode

item.processing: In situ STEM heating, heating rate 1 K s⁻¹
item.structure_change: Progressive loss of smallest NPs (2–4 nm); widening of size distribution up to 13 nm; NPs reshape from elliptical to spherical
item.property_change: Size distribution widens; NP density decreases; shape ratio increases (elliptical to spherical)
item.attributed_mechanism: Coalescence phenomena activate above 673 K; thermo-activated growth mechanisms
quotes: Thermo‐activated growth mechanisms lead to the progressive loss of the smallest NPs (between 2 and 4 nm) and a widening of the size distribution up to 13 nm, at 973 K

item.intervention: Heating to 773 K for several minutes
item.processing: In situ STEM heating, heating rate 1 K s⁻¹

item.property_change: NPs merge; segregation of Au and Cu at surface of coalesced structures; non-coalesced 5 nm NPs remain homogeneous
item.attributed_mechanism: Coalescence phenomena speed up; atomic diffusion segregates Au and Cu at surface, but Janus configuration only in coalesced structures

item.processing: In situ STEM heating, heating rate 1 K s⁻¹

item.processing: In situ STEM heating, heating rate 1 K s⁻¹
item.structure_change: All NPs reduce in size within first minutes; complete loss of Au and Cu from NPs; remaining Co, Ni, Pt remain homogeneous and crystalline FCC
item.property_change: Size reduction of 22% of all observed NPs within first minutes; complete loss of Au and Cu; composition of NPs becomes Co-Ni-Pt ternary
item.attributed_mechanism: Atomic diffusion active enough to drive phase separation; segregation of Au and Cu at surface followed by melting and evaporation of Au-Cu shell
quotes: At 973 K, atomic diffusion is active enough to drive a phase separation in all nanostructures
we measure a size reduction of 22% of all the observed NPs within the first minutes at 973 K
Accordingly, a complete loss of gold and copper is evidenced by STEM‐EDS, while at lower temperatures the composition of NPs was quite stable

item.base_system: 4 nm icosahedral AuCoCuNiPt NP (2057 atoms) in MD simulation
item.intervention: Temperature increase from 500 K to 1500 K
item.processing: MD simulations using LAMMPS, EAM potential, NVT ensemble, 1 fs timestep
item.structure_change: At 500 K: solid solution with random distribution; at 900 K: Au and Cu enriched zones appear at surface; at 1000-1200 K: surface layer essentially Au-Cu; complete solid-to-liquid transition
item.property_change: Surface concentration of Au increases to ≈90% by 900 K; Ni and Co drop below 0.1% at 1000 K; Pt near zero at surface
item.attributed_mechanism: Cohesion effect (lowest surface energies of Au and Cu) drives segregation; surface energy difference between surface and bulk atoms is major driving force
quotes: At low temperatures (500 K), a solid solution is clearly identified: the atoms are distributed in a fully random distribution within a perfectly crystalline NP displaying (111) facets
As the temperature increases, gold‐ and copper‐enriched zones appear at the surface of the NP

Last, ≈1000 K the concentration of nickel and cobalt atoms drops drastically (below 0.1%), while that of platinum is close to zero giving rise to a surface layer consisting essentially of gold and copper

item.base_system: 4 nm icosahedral AuCoCuNiPt NP (2057 atoms) in MD simulation
item.intervention: Temperature increase from 800 K to 1100 K
item.structure_change: At 800 K: bimodal energy distribution for all metals (bulk vs surface); at 1100 K: Au and Cu surface atoms increase at expense of bulk; almost complete depletion of Au in core
item.property_change: Local energy distribution shows Co, Ni, Pt have much lower energy in bulk than surface; Au and Cu have smaller energy difference, favoring surface presence
item.attributed_mechanism: Surface energy, linked to energy difference between surface and bulk atoms, is major driving force behind segregation; Au and Cu have lower surface energies
quotes: At 800 K, a bimodal distribution consisting of two sub‐populations is observed for all metals
As for Pt, only a single population can be identified, namely that of the bulk at very low energies
In case of Au and Cu atoms, this difference in energy is much smaller boosting their presence at the surface

item.base_system: Two icosahedral AuCoCuNiPt NPs (2869 atoms each) in MD simulation
item.structure_change: Coalescence occurs after few ps; resulting NP surface highly enriched in Cu and Au; Au segregation more pronounced than in single NP
item.property_change: Higher Au concentration at surface in coalesced structure compared to single NP; higher self-diffusivity of Au in neck region
item.attributed_mechanism: Reshaping of nanostructures boosts atomic diffusion; neck region presents strong interdiffusion activity to reduce surface curvature
quotes: As seen in Figure 6 a–f , coalescence occurs, after a few ps, with the formation of a NP whose surface is again highly enriched in copper and gold atoms
Interestingly, the Au segregation is more important in the case of the structure resulting from coalescence than for the single icosahedron
Furthermore, a higher D self is revealed in the neck region close to the interface between the two NPs

item.intervention: Comparison with CoPt, AuCu, and Au NPs
item.processing: In situ TEM observations of NPs prepared by PLD on amorphous substrate
item.structure_change: Reshaping and coalescence observed at 673 K in HENA; observed above 873 K in CoPt, AuCu, and Au NPs
item.property_change: HENA shows reshaping/coalescence at lower temperature than subsystems; indicates higher atomic mobility in HENA
item.attributed_mechanism: Lattice distortions and crystal defects in HENA do not induce sluggish diffusion kinetics; atomic diffusion in HENA is more active than in monometallic/bimetallic subsystems
quotes: Surprisingly, our in situ TEM observations show that reshaping and coalescence processes are observed at only 673 K in the present HENA, whereas they are observed above 873 K in CoPt, AuCu, and Au NPs

this direct comparison with metallic and bimetallic NPs fabricated in the same PLD chamber confirms that the lattice distortions and the many crystal defects in the AuCoCuNiPt nanoalloys do not induce sluggish diffusion kinetics
atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems

item.base_system: AuCoCuNiPt NPs fabricated by PLD at 873 K
item.processing: In situ heating and MD simulations
item.structure_change: Out-of-equilibrium FCC solid solution tends toward phase-separated thermodynamic equilibrium; formation of core-shell structure with Au-Cu shell
item.property_change: FCC structure governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy stabilization; phase separation occurs over time
item.attributed_mechanism: Fabrication time (≈12 min) shorter than time required to form core-shell structure; annealing allows system to reach thermodynamic equilibrium stabilized by surface effects
quotes: Thus, our results raise the question: what is the true thermodynamic equilibrium of nanoparticles?
Contrary to what their name suggests, the FCC structure observed in the present HENA fabricated by PLD at 873 K is governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy stabilization
Under annealing, this out‐of‐equilibrium FCC solid solution tends toward a phase‐separated thermodynamic equilibrium that is stabilized by surface effects

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: AuCoCuNiPt NPs fabricated by PLD at 873 K. Intervention: Annealing (time > fabrication time). Processing: In situ heating and MD simulations. Test conditions: 873 K, annealing time > 12 min. Structure change: Out-of-equilibrium FCC solid solution tends toward phase-separated thermodynamic equilibrium; formation of core-shell structure with Au-Cu shell. Property change: FCC structure governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy stabilization; phase separation occurs over time. Mechanism: Fabrication time (≈12 min) shorter than time required to form core-shell structure; annealing allows system to reach thermodynamic equilibrium stabilized by surface effects. item.intervention: Re-evaluation of thermal stability for high-temperature applications
item.processing: Combined in situ STEM and MD simulations
item.structure_change: Phase separation and evaporation of Au-Cu shell at high temperature; poor structural stability
item.property_change: Lowering of temperature range of application; ruling out existence of sluggish diffusion
item.attributed_mechanism: Kinetic effects play key role; phase separation driven by atomic diffusion and surface energy minimization; surface effects govern structural properties
quotes: Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature
Besides ruling out the existence of sluggish diffusion in AuCoCuNiPt nanoalloys and lowering their temperature range of application
this study calls into question the use of AuCoCuNiPt HENA for high‐temperature applications
